paragraphs.text: A loose [raw pu’er](sheng:identity) from Yunnan, dated 1930 and now in powdered form. How it was first made is not recorded. It predates the [state factories](sheng:history): the private tea houses were folded into them only after 1949, when pu’er began to be made to standard recipes.

At ninety-six years it is far past both the ten years some count as [aged raw pu’er](sheng:ageing) and the twenty or more that many wait for. Its form matters to how a tea changes. A tight cake ages slowly and loose leaf faster, because [pressing](sheng:pressing) sets the pace of ageing.

brewing.text: Young raw pu’er takes water a little off the boil, about 85 to 95°C, because hotter water draws out more of its bitterness; an aged one takes 95°C to boiling. A common start is about 7 grams to 100 ml and a quick rinse of a few seconds, then a first steep of ten to fifteen seconds, adding a few seconds each round. A good raw tea gives eight to ten cups or more.

notice.text: A smoother, thicker, sweeter cup with woody, herbal and camphor notes and something of dried dates or dark fruit.
